title: Service Assurance Playbook — Cross-Team Onboarding & Owner Commitments (Q3 2026)
summary: A compact, pragmatic playbook to onboard product and infra owners into a shared service-assurance process that codifies SLO activation, incremental experimentation, and handoffs. Focused on owner commitments, lightweight gates, sprint-level responsibilities, and a 12-week activation runway.
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a repeatable onboarding and commitment process for cross-functional teams to adopt service-assurance practices at Redwood. The emphasis is on pragmatic, incremental SLO activation that minimizes toil, provides clear owner commitments, and preserves product agility.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: New service or major feature launches, model-serving endpoints, and configuration rollouts that require production-level SLOs or reliability changes.
- Audience: Product/feature owner, ML/Serving owner, infra engineer, SRE partner, solutions engineering (optional), and product support triage lead.

Principles:
1) Incrementalism: ship a minimal, measurable SLO quickly (1–2 weeks) and iterate based on telemetry.
2) Owner-first: product and serving owners sign explicit commitments for each milestone.
3) Lightweight gates: avoid heavy approval steps — use clear pass/fail gates defined by metrics.
4) Observability-as-code: share dashboards, alert rules, and dashboards as tracked artifacts.
5) Post-launch learning: every activation includes a focused 3-week monitoring sprint with retro and action items.

12-week activation runway (templates for small-medium projects):
Week 0: Kickoff (alignment)
- 60-minute kickoff with stakeholders: product, serving, infra, SRE. Capture target user journeys and error budgets.
- Output: Activation charter (one-pager). See template Confluence link.

Weeks 1–2: Baseline & minimal SLO
- Identify critical user flows (2–3). Define a single availability or latency SLO for each (SLO owner = product owner).
- Implement minimal telemetry: alpha dashboard, 1–2 alert rules tuned to symptoms, and synthetic checks if applicable.
- Gate: SLO definition documented and minimal dashboard visible to SRE.

Weeks 3–6: SLO experiment & mitigation hooks
- Run a 3-week experiment: measure real traffic, collect error budget burn, and exercise a mitigation (fallback model, cache warmup, reduced batch sizes).
- Owner commitments: product owns impact assessment, serving owns mitigation implementation, SRE validates alert fidelity and escalation path.
- Gate: <10% false positive alert rate in synthetic tests and owner signoff to continue.

Weeks 7–9: Harden & automate
- Add automated rollbacks or routing fallbacks where feasible. Template runbook added to the repo.
- SLAs and rate limits reviewed with infra.
- Gate: Successful automated rollback simulation in staging OR canary.

Weeks 10–12: Launch & 3-week observation sprint
- Move SLOs to production dashboards; enable paging on high-severity symptoms for initial 3-week observation.
- Conduct weekly short reviews with stakeholders (15–30m) focusing on burn rate and anomalies.
- Deliver a 1-page post-activation retro and action list.

Roles & responsibilities (practical commitments):
- Product / Feature Owner (committer): owns SLO definition, user-impact translations, and final go/no-go.
- Serving/Model Owner: implements mitigation strategies (fallback models, quantization profiles, cache policies), provides rollout knobs.
- Platform/Infra: provides capacity guidance, autoscaling guardrails, and helps run rollback simulations.
- SRE Partner: validator for monitoring, alerting, and escalation topology; curator of runbooks.
- Support / Triage Lead: owns first-line incidents, symphony with on-call rotation.

Lightweight gates (decision checklist for each milestone):
- SLO defined in doc with metric, target, and measurement window. (yes/no)
- Dashboard showing SLI and error budget. (yes/no)
- Alert rules mapped to actionable runbook steps. (yes/no)
- Mitigation strategies implemented or proven in simulation. (yes/no)
- Owner signoffs captured in ticket comments. (yes/no)

Success metrics (what we measure):
- Time to first SLO (goal: <= 2 weeks from kickoff).
- Fraction of activations that surface a remediation within 3 weeks (target: >= 60% for early detection).
- False positive alert rate during experiment (target: < 10%).
- Mean time to restore for SLO-impacting incidents (baseline and target improvement).

TL;DR runbook template (to be copied into feature repo):
- One-line SLO definition.
- Owner contacts (pager, slack).
- Quick recovery steps (3 bullets).
- Escalation path (SRE -> Eng -> Product).
- Postmortem owner and timeline.

Communication and sync cadence:
- Weekly check-ins during experiments (15–30 minutes).
- Daily asynchronous incident updates via shared incident thread for the 3-week observation sprint.
- Post-activation retro within 7 days of observation sprint end.

Risk register (common guardrails and mitigations):
- Alert fatigue: mitigate by pairing each new alert with a runbook step and marking it low/medium/high.
- Model drift surprises: require synthetic dataset probes at deploy time and hourly sampling for the first 72 hours.
- Capacity shocks: autoscaling bump policy with explicit cost ceiling and opt-in burst policy.

Owner commitment template (one-line statements recorded on each ticket):
- "I, <owner>, will deliver SLO definition and minimal dashboard by <date>."
- "I, <serving owner>, will implement the fallback path and verify in staging by <date>."
- "I, <SRE partner>, will validate monitoring and runbook and declare readiness by <date>."

Checklist for handoff to SRE runbook library:
- Dashboard link added to ticket.
- Runbook file created under ops-playbooks/slo-activations/<service>-<date>.md.
- Pager rotation assigned.
- Post-activation retro scheduled.

Examples / micro-patterns (practical templates):
- Latency SLO (tail): p99 < 250ms for endpoint X over 7d rolling window. Measure from edge to model inference complete.
- Availability SLO: successful-response-rate >= 99.5% measured at service gateway after retries.
- Degradation policy: if burn rate > 3x expected and error budget < 20% remain -> enable degraded-mode routing with cached responses.

How to start (quick-start checklist for a product owner):
1) Open a ticket using the activation template.
2) Book the 60m kickoff with SRE and serving.
3) Declare the primary SLI and minimal SLO in the ticket within 48 hours.
4) Attach prototype dashboard or synthetic check.

Known open items / things to iterate on (for the program):
- Auto-generated SLO templates per service type (text generation, embeddings, reranking).
- Better synthetic probes for model semantic correctness (not just latency/availability).
- One-click runbook scaffolding in the repo.

Appendix: useful links and templates
- Activation charter template: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SRE/Activation+Charter+Template
- Runbook template: github.com/redwood-inference/ops-playbooks/tree/main/templates/runbook.md
- SLO definition examples: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SRE/SLO+Examples

Next steps (for this doc):
- Finalize templates and land a one-click ticket template (owners: Priya, Evan) by end of Q3.
- Pilot with 3 teams this quarter: serving runtime, hosted-api product, and a customer integration flow.
- Track and publish activation metrics monthly to the reliability dashboard.

Reviewer notes:
Please comment inline with specific blockers or missing templates. If this process seems too heavy for small features, suggest a trimmed "fast lane" checklist we can standardize.
